rv.q: Play and production are simultaneously a taut distillation and a gripping realisation of a giddying idea that resonates long after the curtain falls.
There is nobody like Caryl Churchill and it's hard to think of any writer in history so completely on top of their game at her age.

John Heffernan rawly embodies the lurches between memories of past closeness and the chasm of cold absence that grief's derangement brings.
The indomitable Churchill proves that small can be mighty, particularly when your work is so innately, and potently, theatrical.

The meticulous rhythm of that list – drawn out with relish by Heffernan – which is poetic and funny, absurd yet somehow touching, characterises the 83-year-old playwright's absolute mastery of her form.
A beautifully staged reflection on the pain of confronting loss and the need to move on by Gary Naylor

cn.t: Caryl Churchill's 20-minute meditation on grief and loss earns acclaim for packing profound themes into a brief runtime. Critics praise the play's theatrical potency, surreal complexity, and the precision of Churchill's language in this visionary work.

vr.q: What follows in this short comedy about loss is both thought-provoking and unexpectedly funny.
